The answer would be clearer if the question explained why the dollar's market share declined. The most likely, and most troublesome, scenario is a decline in the creditworthiness of the US government.
column8: This question is poorly stated. If the dollar is permanently weaker because of a decline in the demand for US government assets, then the costs of financing US deficits would increase. If it is weaker because of an increase in the US savings rate, then the cost would decrease.

column5: By "A sustained decline in the dollar's market share" I interpret decline in demand for US dollar assets by investors. This is not good for the US as a whole as it is borrowing and will have to pay higher rates.
column8: It depends what makes the dollar weaker. The answer is yes if this reflects, again, less demand for US assets, since this drives US interest rates (in foreign currency) up. But the dollar could be weaker for other reasons, e.g. if foreign countries do not want US made goods.
